lessons.title: File descriptors: 0, 1, 2 and the rest
lessons.goal:
Learn that an open file is a small number (a **file descriptor**) in each process, how to open and close descriptors in the shell, and how to see them in `/proc`.

Why it matters: sockets, pipes, files and devices are all descriptors. Redirections, `lsof` output, "too many open files" and deleted-but-open files all make sense once you know this.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. A sample data file is created for the examples.

steps.title: A descriptor is an index
steps.text: When a program opens a file, the kernel returns a small number, the **file descriptor** (fd). The program uses that number in `read` and `write`. Every process starts with 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout) and 2 (stderr). `strace` shows the number returned by `openat`: the **lowest free** number, so 3.

run.cmd: strace -e trace=openat cat data.txt 2>&1 | grep data.txt

steps.title: Open a descriptor in the shell
steps.text: `exec 3< FILE` opens FILE for reading as fd 3 in the current shell. `read -u 3` reads a line from it. The next read continues where the last stopped: the **offset** is stored with the open file.

steps.title: fdinfo shows the offset
steps.text: `/proc/PID/fdinfo/N` shows the current position (`pos`) and flags of descriptor N.

run.cmd: exec 3<&-; [ -e /proc/$$/fd/3 ] && echo 'fd 3 still open' || echo 'fd 3 is closed'

steps.after: `pos: 12` = two lines of 6 bytes were read. `exec 3<&-` closes descriptor 3, so `/proc/PID/fd/3` is gone.

steps.title: Open a descriptor for writing
steps.text: `exec 4> FILE` opens (and truncates) FILE as fd 4. `>&4` sends output there. This is the same mechanism as `> file`, kept open for several commands.

run.cmd: exec 4> out.txt; echo one >&4; echo two >&4; exec 4>&-; cat out.txt

steps.title: Descriptors are not only files
steps.text: Pipes, sockets, terminals and devices are descriptors as well. The link in `/proc/PID/fd` shows what each one is. In a subshell with `/dev/null` open as fd 7:
steps.under: Each process has a **file descriptor table**: an array whose entries point to kernel objects (open file descriptions). `open` picks the lowest free index. `close` frees it. `fork` copies the table, `exec` keeps it (unless the descriptor is marked close-on-exec), which is how redirections reach the new program.

quiz.q: What number does `open` return when only 0, 1 and 2 are in use?
What does `exec 3< file` do in a shell?
options: Opens file as descriptor 3 in the current shell
quiz.explain: It opens the descriptor and keeps it open.

quiz.q: Where can you see the position in an open file?

check.scenario: A script does `exec 3> log.txt` and later `echo done >&3`. A reader wonders why `lsof` shows the file open after the script's `cat` finished. What is happening?
check.answer: The script's shell still holds descriptor 3 open until it exits or runs `exec 3>&-`. `cat` finishing does not close the shell's own descriptor. Close it explicitly when you are done.

lessons.title: Limits: "Too many open files"
lessons.goal:
Learn the per-process and system-wide limits on open files, reproduce the error `Too many open files`, and learn how to look for leaks.

Why it matters: servers with many connections hit this limit (EMFILE) and start refusing clients. It is a top-five production error.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. A sample data file is created for the examples.

steps.title: The soft and hard limit
steps.text: Each process has a **soft** limit (enforced) and a **hard** limit (the ceiling the soft limit may be raised to without root) for open files. `ulimit -n` shows the soft limit, `-Hn` the hard one.

steps.title: A program that opens files until it fails
steps.text: `fdhog.c` opens `/dev/null` in a loop and reports the error.

steps.title: Lower the limit and run it
steps.text: We lower the soft limit to 20 in a subshell. The program has 3 descriptors from the start (0, 1, 2), so it can open 17 more, and then `open` fails with **EMFILE**.

run.output: opened 17 files, then: Too many open files (errno 24)
opened 97 files, then: Too many open files (errno 24)

steps.under: The check is in the kernel: `open` allocates the lowest free fd number and fails with `EMFILE` if that number would be at or above `RLIMIT_NOFILE`. The error text is "Too many open files". There is also a system-wide table: `ENFILE` ("Too many open files in system") when `fs.file-max` is reached.

steps.title: System-wide numbers
steps.text: `/proc/sys/fs/file-nr` has three numbers: allocated file handles, unused, and the system maximum (`fs.file-max`).

steps.title: Look at a running process
steps.text: `/proc/PID/fd` has one entry per open descriptor, so counting entries shows usage. `prlimit` shows or changes limits of a running process.

run.output:
RESOURCE DESCRIPTION                SOFT   HARD UNITS
NOFILE   max number of open files 524288 524288 files

steps.title: Raise the limit for a service
steps.text: For a systemd service set `LimitNOFILE=65536` in the unit. For a login session set `nofile` in `/etc/security/limits.conf`. After a change restart the service and verify in `/proc/PID/limits`. Raising the limit hides a **leak** (descriptors never closed): if the count grows without bound, find the leak.

run.cmd: sleep 100 & p=$!; sudo prlimit --pid $p --nofile=4096:4096; grep 'Max open files' /proc/$p/limits; kill $p

quiz.q: What errno does `open` return when the per-process limit is reached?
Which file shows a running process's limits?
A server hits the limit again after you raised it tenfold. What should you check?
options: Whether descriptors leak (count grows over time)
quiz.explain: A leak makes any limit too small eventually.

quiz.q: How do you set a higher limit for a systemd service?

check.scenario: nginx logs `accept4() failed (24: Too many open files)` under load. Give the steps to fix and verify it.
check.answer: Check the limit of the running master/worker: `cat /proc/PID/limits`, and count `ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l`. Raise `worker_rlimit_nofile` in nginx and `LimitNOFILE=` in the systemd unit (and `fs.file-max` if the system limit is near). Restart, re-check `/proc/PID/limits`. If the count still climbs without load, look for a descriptor leak.

lessons.title: The VFS and the open file description
lessons.goal:
Learn the layers between a `read()` and the disk, and the difference between a descriptor, an open file description and an inode.

Why it matters: it explains why a forked child and its parent share a file offset, why two separate `open` calls do not, and how one interface works for ext4, xfs, NFS, `/proc` and sockets alike.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. A sample data file is created for the examples.

steps.title: Three levels
steps.text:
1. The **file descriptor** is an entry in a process's table.
2. It points to an **open file description** (kernel `struct file`): the offset, the flags, and a pointer to the file's operations.
3. That points to an **inode** (the file itself: size, owner, data location) found through a **dentry** (name).

Several descriptors can point to one description (`dup`, `fork`). Several descriptions can point to one inode (two `open` calls).

run.cmd: exec 3< data.txt; lsof -a -d 3 -p $$ 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==2 {print "lsof shows inode (NODE):", $(NF-1)}'; exec 3<&-

steps.title: Sharing the offset: a test program
steps.text: The program opens the file once and forks: parent and child hold **the same description**, so they share one offset. Then it opens the file twice: two descriptions, two independent offsets.

run.output:
-- one open(), then fork: parent and child share the offset
child    read: alpha
parent   read: bravo
-- two separate open() calls: independent offsets
fd a     read: alpha
fd b     read: alpha

steps.after: The child read `alpha`, then the parent continued with `bravo`. With two `open` calls both descriptors started at the beginning.

steps.title: dup shares a description too
steps.text: `exec 4<&3` duplicates descriptor 3 as 4. Reading from either moves the same offset.

steps.title: The VFS: one interface, many file systems
steps.text: The **Virtual File System** is the kernel layer that defines the common objects (superblock, inode, dentry, file) and a table of operations for each (`read`, `write`, `open`, `lookup`...). Each file system (xfs, ext4, NFS, procfs) fills in its own table. A `read()` on any descriptor calls the `read` entry of that file's table.
steps.under: The path walk is the part you see in `strace` as a single `openat`. The kernel splits the path, finds each component in the **dentry cache** (or asks the file system's `lookup`), crosses mount points, checks permissions on each directory, and finally creates a `struct file`. Cached dentries make repeated opens fast; negative dentries remember names that do not exist.

quiz.q: Which object stores the current read/write offset?
quiz.explain: It is per open file description.

quiz.q: After `fork`, parent and child both read from a descriptor opened before. Do they share the offset?
options: Yes: they share one open file description
Provides a common interface that each file system implements
quiz.explain: A uniform set of objects and operations.

quiz.q: Two separate `open()` calls on one file give...
quiz.explain: Each open creates its own description.

check.scenario: Two processes append log lines to the same file and sometimes lines are interleaved or overwritten. Which open flag makes appends safe and why?
check.answer: `O_APPEND`: the kernel moves the offset to the end **and** writes atomically for each `write()`. Without it, each process uses its own offset and may overwrite the other's data. (Shared descriptors via fork share one offset, but separate `open` calls do not.) Keep each log record in a single `write()` call.

interview.a: A small integer index into a process's table of open files. 0, 1, 2 are stdin, stdout, stderr. See [the lesson](#/lesson/17/file-descriptors).

interview.q: How do you diagnose `Too many open files`?
interview.a: Check `/proc/PID/limits`, count `/proc/PID/fd`, compare with the limit, raise `LimitNOFILE`/`nofile` and look for a descriptor leak (`lsof -p PID`). See [the lesson](#/lesson/17/too-many-open-files).

interview.q: What is the difference between EMFILE and ENFILE?
interview.a: EMFILE: the process reached its own limit. ENFILE: the system-wide file table (`fs.file-max`) is full.

interview.q: Do a parent and a forked child share file offsets?
interview.a: Yes for descriptors opened before the fork: they share the open file description. Files opened separately have independent offsets. See [the lesson](#/lesson/17/vfs-open-file-description).
The kernel's virtual file system layer: common objects (inode, dentry, file, superblock) and operation tables implemented by each file system, so `read`/`write` work the same everywhere.
File descriptors are inherited across `execve` unless marked close-on-exec. The shell sets the descriptors before it execs the program.

glossary.def: A small integer that identifies an open file, pipe or socket within a process.
Error: the process has too many open files.
The per-process limit on open file descriptors.
The kernel object that holds the offset and flags of an open file; shared by dup and fork.
The file system object that stores a file's metadata and data location.
Virtual File System: the kernel layer that gives all file systems one interface.
A cached directory entry that maps a name to an inode.
